title: Top 8 WORST Lifts for Hypertrophy (and why you should still do them)
summary: Responding to an article listing 'bad' hypertrophy lifts, he takes each one (deadlift, barbell row, good morning, Smith squat, upright row, rack pull, landmine press, plank) and explains how to program it so its weaknesses become strengths. Core message: lifts work in combination and as accessories; 'do this not that' content is fear-mongering.
claims: The 'do this not that' trend fear-mongers lifts that built great physiques for decades and sells a flawless replacement that doesn't exist
The deadlift's flaws (no eccentric stretch, high fatigue, poor stimulus-to-fatigue) are real but only a problem if you program it badly; keep floor deadlift volume minimal
Fatigue is also stimulus: cut deadlift sets and reps until you get just enough fatigue to grow without being wrecked
Because the deadlift hits many muscles diffusely, use it to open a back/posterior-chain lower day, then focus on the muscles you want to grow
Bodybuilders should treat the deadlift as an accessory to the Romanian deadlift: RDLs give far better stimulus-to-fatigue with a stretch, but stall on the concentric, which the deadlift trains
Get most hinge volume from RDLs and use the deadlift for intensity on the concentric only
The barbell row is a full-body compound with lower back stress and leg drive by design; don't expect it to isolate the upper back
Open sessions with barbell rows like a deadlift, with higher reps and volume, then move to isolation that removes lower back and legs; don't bury rows after squats and a heavy hinge
Rules like never putting more than two plates on a good morning are arbitrary nonsense; it is a great lift for hamstrings, glutes, lower back and upper back
Use a safety squat bar for good mornings: best feel and strength curve
There is no dangerous lift: a good morning is a hip hinge like a stiff-leg deadlift, and it is up to you to adapt it
You don't need your back parallel to the floor on good mornings; hinge only as deep as feels comfortable
With higher reps and RIR the lower back is fine: he did 245-255 lb good mornings for 8, 7 and 6 reps at 2 RIR and only his hamstrings were tired
Novices should avoid the Smith squat and learn proprioception under free weights; the Smith is for those who have mastered the compounds

The Smith's fixed path lets you put the feet forward, which raises quad activation, lowers back strain and for some raises glute activation; useful for back injuries or extra leg volume without a hack or belt squat
Upright row fears are overblown: injuries come from loading it too heavy with a big-mover mindset
Bodybuilders sometimes must put themselves at a disadvantage; light weight taken to failure in a low rep range still grows muscle
Treat the upright row like a lateral raise, 10-15 reps; few people ever need more than about 130 lb
Adding 5-15 lb to an isolation lift like curls is significant progress
Isometric stretch for the upper back and traps is highly underrated
Rack pull from below the knee, touch-and-go with a controlled negative, and hold the last rep until you can't; uses less weight than his deadlift and carries over to all pulls
The landmine press 'instability' argument is invalid; it is a hybrid between vertical and horizontal pressing, best used as an accessory to the overhead press
He pressed a forest log landmine-style for several days and it felt great on shoulders and triceps
Planks are hard to progress, lack stretch and are redundant with bracing on compounds, so he programs them on upper body days
If you're too strong for planks, do them at the end of the workout in a giant-set circuit
Deadlifts and RDLs are each inferior alone but strong combined; minimalist routines fail
After honestly trying a lift and finding it doesn't work for you, you can drop it into your exercise graveyard; the problem is group-think declaring lifts bad
